questions.q: Besides forgetting to shift a signal, which of these is also a form of look-ahead bias?
options: Using a 10-day moving average instead of a 20-day moving average
Tuning a strategy's parameters by testing against the entire historical dataset and picking the best-performing combination, then reporting performance on that same dataset
Trading a highly liquid large-cap stock
Charging a 10 bps transaction cost
questions.explain: Selecting parameters using the full dataset (including what is 'future' relative to earlier points in that period) and then evaluating on the same data means the reported performance partly reflects fitting to that specific data, not an honest forward test.

questions.q: Why does building a backtest universe from 'today's S&P 500 constituents' and applying it to a backtest starting in 2005 create survivorship bias?
options: Because the S&P 500 only contains 500 companies
Because it silently excludes companies that were in the index in 2005 but have since been delisted, acquired, or removed for underperforming, which systematically inflates measured returns
Because index membership never changes over time
Because large-cap stocks always outperform small-cap stocks
questions.explain: Using today's membership list retroactively removes exactly the companies that failed or underperformed and were removed from the index — on average the worst performers — inflating the backtested average return.

questions.q: What is a point-in-time universe, and why does it fix survivorship bias?
options: A universe of only the most liquid instruments
A record of which instruments were actually tradable members of a universe as of each specific historical date, including ones that have since disappeared
A universe that updates in real time but ignores history entirely
A universe limited to a single point in time, such as today
questions.explain: A point-in-time universe reflects actual historical membership at each date, including companies that were later delisted or removed, so the backtest doesn't silently erase historical failures.

questions.q: What is the common structural property shared by look-ahead bias and survivorship bias?
options: Both make backtested results look randomly different, with no consistent direction
Both make a backtest's reported performance look better than what a trader living through history in real time could actually have achieved
Both only affect options and derivatives strategies
Both are impossible to avoid in any backtest
questions.explain: Look-ahead bias imports future information into a decision; survivorship bias imports foreknowledge of which instruments survive into the universe construction. Both systematically bias results upward, not randomly.

questions.q: A dataset contains a company's GDP or fundamental figure that was later revised, but the historical dataset only stores the corrected (final) value on all dates, including before the correction happened. What problem does this create?
options: No problem — corrected data is always more accurate to use
A form of look-ahead bias, since a decision on an earlier date would be using information (the correction) that didn't actually exist at that time
This is only a problem for cryptocurrency data
It creates survivorship bias, not look-ahead bias
questions.explain: If the dataset reflects the post-correction value on dates before the correction was actually published, a backtest trading on that date is using information that wasn't yet available — a form of look-ahead bias, not survivorship bias.
